https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: More than 80 dead and dying greater crested terns have been spotted off the South Australian coast in what is a suspected H5N1 bird flu mass mortality event. Photograph: imageBROKER/David & Micha Sheldon/Getty Images/imageBROKER RF View image in fullscreen More than 80 dead and dying greater crested terns have been spotted off the South Australian coast in what is a suspected H5N1 bird flu mass mortality event. Photograph: imageBROKER/David & Micha Sheldon/Getty Images/imageBROKER RF Bird flu First Australian mass mortality event suspected as deadly bird flu virus rapidly escalates among native birds Helicopter surveillance finds dead and dying greater crested terns off South Australian coast as H5 virus spreads Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Graham Readfearn Environment and climate correspondent Sat 1 Aug 2026 02.12 EDT Last modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 04.20 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More than 80 dead and sick birds seen on rocks off the South Australian coast are suspected to be the first mass mortality event from the deadly H5N1 bird flu virus, only six weeks after the disease arrived in Australia. Authorities reported on Saturday that helicopter surveillance had revealed 49 dead greater crested terns on Baudin Rocks, near Robe, as well as 35 more sick terns. While some of the birds had been collected for testing, South Australia’s chief vet Skye Freuan said it was likely the first mass mortality event from the disease. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email South Australia also reported three suspected positive cases in other greater crested terns, including one inland at Monarto, suggesting the disease has begun moving away from the coast. The Monarto area is home to several poultry farms. Three silver gulls were also suspected positive, SA authorities said, adding to the first silver gull found a few days ago and confirmed positive by the CSIRO earlier on Saturday. Kate Millar, the chief executive of conservation charity BirdLife Australia, called it a “very significant escalation of the bird flu situation in Australia, and a very bleak milestone”. “Sadly, we’re at the beginning of a long and challenging battle and birds and wildlife are going to need all the help they can get,” she said. Jack Gough, the chief executive of the Invasive Species Council, said it now appeared the disease was “starting to take off” and “mirroring the experience in South America of early detections, then rapid increases in numbers and spread leading to mass mortality events in wildlife.” “We are still at the very early stages of this devastating disease spreading, but the possible first mass mortality coming just days after the virus was declared not eradicable indicates how quickly this could escalate,” he said. Freuan said there was “nothing we can do” to stop the spread of the disease, but that surveillance was working. The news came at the end of a significant week in the development of the disease when numbers jumped by 20 in just a few days to the current total of 53. Australia was the last continent to have the unwelcome arrival of a disease that has killed millions of birds and mammals around the world. Victoria this week confirmed its first cases of the virulent strain in a greater crested tern found in Portland, with the state joining Western Australia, South Australia, New South Wales and Queensland that have all recorded positive cases. On Saturday, Victorian authorities said samples from five crested terns had been sent to the CSIRO laboratory in Geelong, with preliminary testing suggesting more positive results. Five confirmed cases in birds at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island also raised concerns for the welfare of the area’s Australian sea lions – an endangered species. Tens of thousands of seals have died worldwide from the disease. But it has been the cases among silver gulls that has experts like Sean Dooley, the national affairs adviser at BirdLife Australia, concerned that the spread of the virus has now reached a critical new stage. “When people think of a seagull, they’re almost always thinking of the silver gull,” said Dooley. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Australian sea lions, an endangered species, are at risk of contracting H5N1 bird flu. Photograph: Brad Leue/Alamy “They’re very common, and primarily they are coastal, but they do come inland and can turn up in Lake Eyre following floods,” said Dooley. Silver gulls are the second Australian native species to catch the disease, after dozens of detections in greater crested terns. But it is the silver gull’s behaviour and habits that have experts concerned because they scavenge from dead or dying animals, meaning they can easily pick up the disease from other sick birds. They also pick detritus from water bodies – lakes and flooded areas included – and these are known to be breeding grounds for the disease. “There is such a large population of silver gulls, and they move into other habitats. They could be the vector that takes bird flu inland,” says Dooley. “They’re also really successful in urban areas and could bring the disease into those bird populations.” Because Australia has a high concentration of unique birds, the susceptibility of many native species isn’t known. But the fears are there is no reason to think they would manage any better than birds overseas. Birds that flock around water have tended to be the hardest hit. Examples include sandwich terns, black-headed gulls and northern gannets in Europe and, in Peru, pelicans. Dooley said the mood at BirdLife Australia this week had been one of “trying to suppress that sinking, gut-churning feeling”. The winter season for birdwatchers along the coast had been one of the best in 10 years, said Dooley, with rare petrels turning up in numbers along the east coast. “Now that has been heavily tinged because probably among those were birds carrying H5N1.” Explore more on these topics Bird flu Wildlife Birds Marine life Animals news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Environment Climate crisis Wildlife Energy Pollution Green light

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cz05.text: Image source, Supplied Image caption, The body of an Indian climber who died 30 years ago wearing his green mountaineering boots has become a grim marker along the road to Everest's summit By Jehangir Ali BBC News Hindi ,Â Reporting from Skurbuchan, Ladakh Published 6 hours ago For 30 years, a dead body known as "Green Boots" has been lying in the snow, nestled under an overhanging rock, not far from Mount Everest's summit. The lime mountaineering boots worn by an Indian climber who died in 1996 have been a grim trail marker for many climbers on their way up the world's highest peak ever since. Now India is looking for a specialist high-altitude recovery team to undertake a complex and risky mission to retrieve what they say is Dorje Morup's body â arguably the most famous of the hundreds whose bodies have been left frozen on the mountain. They hope they are on the cusp of returning his remains to friends and family who never gave up hope he'd come home. "On some days, before I went to sleep, I would think that there'd be a knock on the door tonight and that when I opened, he would be there," Morup's wife told the BBC. "When he comes home, I will ask him: 'Where were you all these years?'" Disaster struck on descent Image source, Family handout Image caption, Dorje Morup was a keen mountaineer and had climbed many peaks, including Stok Kangri, the highest peak in the Ladakh mountain range The night before he left to be part of a historic Indian expedition on Everest, Morup sat with his wife at his home in Ladakh, an Indian-administered territory in another part of the Himalayas. He made her a promise: that he would come back a hero and make his country proud. "He asked me to take care of the kids and come to the airport to greet him on his return," Konchak Yangskit told the BBC at her home. A lance naik, or lance corporal, in the Indo Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), the force guarding much of India's border with China, 48-year-old Morup was no stranger to Himalayan trekking. But Yangskit says she had a strange sense of foreboding that night: "I wondered if I was ever going to see him again." Morup was one of six climbers on the ITBP expedition attempting to reach the top of Everest â which lies on the border between Nepal and the Chinese-governed territory of Tibet. Most climbers choose to ascend from the Nepalese side, but Morup's crew wanted to write their names into the history books as the first Indian expedition to do it from the treacherous Chinese side. Image caption, Morup's wife, Yangskit, says because she never saw his body, she found it difficult to believe he was dead Three out of six members of the expedition turned back due to a snowstorm, but Morup and two others - Tsewang Smanla and Tsewang Paljor â kept struggling, all the way up to the 8,849m summit. Disaster, a blizzard, struck as they descended and killed all three. Like many of the more than 300 people who have died in the Everest region since records began a century ago, their bodies remain on the mountain. Two have never been found, but the third body - that of "Green Boots" - has been lying frozen in the snow for three decades at an altitude of 8,500 metres. For years, it was assumed that "Green Boots" was another member of the expedition, Tsewang Paljor. But testimony from surviving members of the 1996 expedition and the location of the last radio contact with the climbers have now led authorities to believe the remains belong to Morup. Image source, Family handout Image caption, Morup's family is proud to show the certificate issued by the Chinese government confirming he had successfully reached the top of Everest An ITBP official, speaking anonymously because he is not authorised to speak to the media, told BBC News Hindi that Morup's clothes and climbing gear helped officials identify the body in recent years. Since then, they've been plotting how to get their comrade home so they can confirm his identity beyond doubt through DNA testing and offer his family a semblance of closure. "We never forgot him. It was only a matter of time," the ITBP official said. How difficult will it be to recover the body? Retrieving those who have died on the mountain is a dangerous, gruelling task, and, up until the past decade, very rare. Many of the bodies, like Morup's, are in what climbers call Everest's death zone â where temperatures can plunge to -40C and oxygen levels are about a third of those at sea level. "The weather and snow conditions are going to be crucial," said Tshiring Jangbu Sherpa, a prominent Nepalese mountaineer who has taken part in other recovery missions. "The north side has fewer crevasses, but it is riskier. If something bad happens from the Nepalese side, you get quickly evacuated by helicopter. But there is no such system from the Chinese side," he told BBC Hindi. Image caption, Some of photos of Morup and a few of his belongings have helped his family keep his memory alive The Chinese side of the peak â where Green Boots' body is â is steeper and doesn't have the same support structures as the southern slope, which is another complicating factor, Sherpa sources have told BBC News Nepali. "It's really tough to get that body down even in popular spring season, let alone the autumn [which has more unpredictable weather]. That's the simple reason it is still there for so many years," mountaineering guide Pemba Ongchu Sherpa said. "There would need to be 10 to 12 climbers who are capable of making summits, just to fix [support] ropes to reach that point." Green Boots will also have to be physically carried down to an altitude where it can be collected by a helicopter, or possibly yaks, and transported back to an airport â a job which also requires huge manpower. Sherpas say bodies shrouded in iced-up climbing gear often weigh several times the average man and are frequently frozen into awkward positions, making bringing them down the challenging terrain even more treacherous. The remains may also begin defrosting and decomposing once they reach lower altitudes. The start of the descent with the body would be the most difficult, Indian climber Kuntal Joisher told BBC Nepali. "It's going to be very, very risky endeavour. It's extremely steep ground with lots of rock. Logistically, this [first] 1000m is going to be a humungous challenge." "The main thing is to not put Sherpa lives at risk for a dead body." All of this makes for a hugely expensive recovery mission â experts say even the most straightforward ones cost between $40,000 and $80,000, a sum beyond the means of most families. It is more common for local teams to move people who have died out of view on the mountain: like explorer Francys Arsentiev, dubbed the Sleeping Beauty of Everest, who in 2007 was moved to a more private final resting place on Everest almost a decade after she died. But the ITBP â which is funding the recovery operation â wants Morup's body to be returned by September, and is looking for mountain rescue Sherpa groups who could do the job. Once returned to India, the body will undergo DNA testing and, if confirmed to be Morup, his remains will be given back to his family. 'My heart refused to believe he had died' For years, Morup's family back in Ladakh have struggled to come to terms with his disappearance. Now around 75, Yangskit struggles to recall even the day she was married. But the days after the tragedy remain etched in her mind. "I only knew there was a storm on the mountain. Even though we organised cremation prayers at home, my heart refused to believe he had died," she says with tears rolling down her face. "I didn't see his dead body, so it was difficult for me to believe it." Image caption, Morup's family remains cautious about what the body being returned will mean for them Image caption, Morup's eldest son, Punchok Dorjai, looks up at a framed photo of his father All that remains of Morup today are his medals and trophies, a couple of old photos from his mountain adventures â and, most importantly, a certificate from the Chinese government which states that at 17:30 on 10 May 1996, Morup reached the top of Everest. If the recovery mission is successful, Morup's son Punchok Dorjai told the BBC that the family would hold a funeral for him near the Martyrs Park in Ladakh's capital Leh. "My father gave his life for the country and he should be remembered as a martyr," Dorjai said, adding that his teammates who perished deserve the same title. The family will also proudly save a symbol of Morup's legacy at their home, to go alongside his summit certification, he said: "We are planning to keep the Green Boots." https://mishpacha.com/missing-the-points.text: For over five years, Rav Chaim Brisker stood at the center of efforts to create an international organization for Torah Jewry, but at the founding conference of Agudas Yisrael in 1912, he presented 18 conditions for his participation and left with no resolution. Negotiations continued, and his relationship with the movement remained disputed. But where was that list? Over a century later, the clues are finally coming together A t the end of Tishrei last year, Rabbi Shimon Yosef Meller, the longtime chronicler of the Brisk dynasty and author of a multivolume biography of Rav Chaim Soloveitchik, gathered together with some 150 visitors at Rav Chaim’s kever in Warsaw’s Jewish cemetery. Rabbi Meller had brought with him the completed manuscript of the third volume of Rabban shel Kol Bnei Hagolah . After speaking about the venerated figure buried before them, he placed the manuscript on the kever and asked mechilah for anything he might have misunderstood or recorded inaccurately. It wasn’t mechilah to be taken lightly: In the latter part of the 19th century, in the small Russian town of Volozhin, Rav Chaim HaLevi Soloveitchik was attracting some of the brightest minds from across the Jewish communities of Eastern Europe in an innovative method of Talmud study that would become known as the “Brisker derech ” — cutting through complex arguments and webs of counterproofs with clearcut halachic definitions and categorizations. Following the closure of the Volozhin yeshivah in 1892, Rav Chaim took up a rabbinical position in the town of Brisk. There he soon emerged as one of the foremost rabbinic leaders of his day, working for nearly three decades as a staunch advocate on behalf of the downtrodden Jews of the Russian Empire, and was steadfast in his refusal to allow secularization, nationalism, or tyranny to sweep away the great institutions of Torah life and learning. The crowd answered, “ Machul lach .” Yet as they began to disperse, Rabbi Meller was approached by a man he didn’t recognize. “Rabbi Meller,” the man asked, “does the new volume include Rav Chaim’s Eighteen Points?” Rabbi Meller stopped. The question touched a subject that had frustrated him for years. The “Yud-Ches Devarim” was a document of near-mythic importance in Brisk: Eighteen conditions Rav Chaim had demanded during the founding of Agudas Yisrael. People quoted individual clauses in his name. Historians debated them. For Agudah, Rav Chaim’s early involvement testified to the movement’s Torah foundations; in Brisk, the failure to accept his conditions explained why he formally left it. But the stakes went beyond the old argument over whether Rav Chaim Brisker was Agudah’s founder or dissenter. The Eighteen Points addressed the larger question at the heart of the nascent movement: What kind of organization was Agudah going to be? The conditions were, in effect, Rav Chaim’s blueprint for the powers and limits of organized Torah Jewry. And the question of how collective chareidi power coexists with independent Torah authority has hardly disappeared. For Rabbi Meller, though, the issue was more technical. He had spent years looking for this list — through archives, collectors, and whatever leads came his way — and had finally accepted that his biography would appear without it. “No,” he told the stranger. “I never found it.” The man scribbled a telephone number. “Call me when you get back to Eretz Yisrael,” he said. “Perhaps I can help you.” The book Rabbi Meller had brought to Rav Chaim’s kever , it turned out, was no longer a finished manuscript. Who’s in Charge? To understand why that question stopped Rabbi Meller in his tracks, let’s go back more than a century, to a time when Torah Jewry faced new existential threats, but had no international organization through which to confront them. The Zionist movement had developed international institutions, newspapers, and funding networks. Across Eastern Europe, new ideologies were attracting young Jews away from the beis medrash. Torah-loyal communities fought to preserve their traditional insular approach, but largely as separate towns and organizations. Many rabbanim and chassidic rebbes — including Rav Sholom Dovber Schneersohn (the Rebbe Rashab of Lubavitch), a close friend and associate of the litvish Rav Chaim Brisker who worked in tandem with him to counteract decrees by the Czarist regime — were deeply concerned that secular nationalism would replace mesorah as the foundation of Jewish identity. There was no international body capable of speaking or acting for European Orthodox Jewry as a whole. Earlier attempts to establish international Orthodox associations in Eastern Europe had foundered. The czarist authorities viewed organized Jewish activity with suspicion, while Germany offered far greater freedom to organize. There, Orthodox communities also had decades of experience building institutions to contend with Reform and assimilation. Among the men of leadership attempting to create a new international body were Rav Yaakov Rosenheim, who would lead Agudas Yisrael for four decades; Rav Yitzchak Isaac Halevy (Rabinowitz), author of Doros Harishonim ; and Rav Shlomo Zalman Breuer, rav of Frankfurt’s Adath Jeshurun community and son-in-law of Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch. But the story did not begin in Germany. Contemporary correspondence shows that Rav Chaim’s role was substantive, even as the organizers understood that his name and presence would give the enterprise credibility across Eastern Europe. In a 1990 Jewish Observer article, Rabbi Moshe Kolodny of the Agudath Israel Archives published an English translation of Rav Chaim Ozer Grodzenski’s July 1923 account in the Yiddish newspaper Der Yid . It was Rav Chaim Ozer’s intervention in a public exchange over Rav Chaim’s relationship with Agudah, written in response to Rav Moshe Soloveitchik without naming him. Eleven years after Katowice, the argument exploded into public view. At a 1923 gathering of Mizrachi rabbanim, Rav Moshe Soloveitchik declared that no one could persuade the Orthodox community that his father had supported Agudah. Agudah’s newspaper answered with an attack and printed the 1917 proclamation bearing Rav Chaim’s signature. Rav Moshe replied immediately, challenging the document’s meaning and publishing two of what he called his father’s 13 conditions. Rav Chaim Ozer then entered the dispute with a detailed history of Rav Chaim’s role — without mentioning Rav Moshe by name. The missing conditions had become evidence in a living battle over Rav Chaim’s legacy. Rav Chaim Ozer’s account pushed the story back five years before Katowice, to 1907. “In the year 5667 [1907], the initial meeting was held,” he wrote. Present were Rav Chaim Brisker, Rav Eliezer Gordon of Telz, and Rav Chaim Ozer himself. At that meeting, Rav Chaim Ozer wrote, it was resolved to found an organization called “Knesses Yisrael.” A program was subsequently developed in Vilna and submitted to Rav Chaim Brisker, Rav Dovid Friedman of Karlin, and Rav Eliyahu Chaim Meisel of Lodz. According to Rav Chaim Ozer, their approval was unanimous, and Knesses Yisrael even received government recognition before pressure from the czarist authorities forced its activities to be suspended. That initiative, although eventually aborted, is an important missing piece in the Agudah story. The idea of organizing Torah Jewry across communal boundaries was already being pursued by the leading rabbanim of Russia and Lithuania, with Rav Chaim Brisker at its center. Two years later, in 1909, the effort moved westward. On the initiative of Rav Yitzchak Isaac Halevy, a low-profile conference convened at Bad Homburg, bringing together leading rabbinic figures from Eastern and Central Europe, including Rav Chaim Brisker, Rav Chaim Ozer, Rav Eliezer Gordon, Rav Eliezer Rabinowitz of Minsk, the Gerrer Rebbe, the rav of Bendin, and several Hungarian rabbanim. The Rebbe Rashab, who, together with Rav Chaim, was deeply invested in the collective efforts to protect traditional Jewish education and communal life during this tumultuous era, didn’t attend the meeting in person, but sent a representative to speak on his behalf. Rav Chaim, according to Rav Chaim Ozer’s report, was not recruited merely to lend his name and stature to the program. The correspondence surrounding the meeting indicates that he helped determine who should participate. The goal was to unite traditional, Torah-observant Jewry against the rising tides of secularization, the Enlightenment, and political Zionism. (Rav Chaim’s opposition was directed at the Zionist movement, not Eretz Yisrael itself. He advised institutions of the Old Yishuv and closely questioned visiting meshulachim about its spiritual needs and daily life.) These efforts, as Rav Chaim Ozer described in his 1923 report, laid the initial structural and ideological groundwork for what would officially launch three years later in 1912 as Agudas Yisrael at the Katowice Conference. At the Katowice Conference, the question that would dominate Rav Chaim’s relationship with Agudah came to the fore: Not simply whether Orthodox Jewry should organize, but who would control the organization once it existed. Rav Chaim, Rav Chaim Ozer wrote, “continued to insist that a Moetzes Gedolei HaTorah be established immediately, to supervise the activities of the organization.” His particular fear was that the German educational system of “ Torah im derech eretz ” — a lifesaver for Orthodox German Jewry in the face of the entrenched and aggressive Reform movement — would penetrate the Talmud Torahs and yeshivos of the East, which he regarded as a danger to Torah learning. (Rav Chaim had already lived through the closure of Volozhin due to the insistence of the Russian government to institute secular studies.) But Rav Chaim was not merely registering an objection. He was trying to build the mechanism that would prevent it. And that makes the next stage easier to understand. Three years after Bad Homburg, in 1912, Rav Chaim Brisker traveled to the decisive founding conference in Katowice. Even the journey to Katowice nearly failed before it began. Rav Yaakov Zalman Lipschitz of Brisk wrote to Rav Yitzchak Isaac Halevy that he was weak and suffered heart palpitations, but Rav Chaim would not travel without him. Lipschitz agreed to go because he knew what Rav Chaim’s presence meant. Rav Chaim, he wrote, would be the conference’s living spirit; his judgment would ensure that nothing imperfect emerged, and his name would draw the yerei’im . Without him, Lipschitz feared, most of the “ yerei Shamayim ” would keep their distance. Some 230 rabbanim and communal leaders from across the Jewish world converged there: chassidic rebbes alongside Lithuanian roshei yeshivah, representatives of Eretz Yisrael beside delegates from Germany and Eastern Europe. The Jewish press recorded the excitement over Rav Chaim’s arrival. Even Hatzefirah , the voice of the Maskilim, described German Jews who had never seen him waiting with reverence and curiosity for the man they regarded as the symbol of the Russian rabbinate. When his train arrived, the waiting delegates surrounded the weary rav and accompanied him to his hotel. During the conference, another report noted, his room became a gathering place for delegates eager to see him. But by then, the question was no longer whether Rav Chaim would lend Agudah his prestige. He had been involved in attempts to create such an organization since at least 1907, and had already pushed for the Moetzes that would govern its religious direction. The question at Katowice was whether the organization being born would actually operate on those terms. Price of Partnership Because Rav Chaim had come with conditions. Eighteen of them. The founders of Agudas Yisrael shared a goal: to create a serious international framework for Torah Jewry. But agreement on the goal didn’t erase some profound differences among the delegates. The Orthodox community in Germany had developed under the banner of Torah im derech eretz . Its educational structure included secular studies, an approach its leaders saw as a necessary response to the conditions around them. But what protected one community from assimilation could endanger another. The gedolim of Eastern Europe feared that once a single organization linked the communities of East and West, a German accommodation might become a program exported into the chadarim and yeshivos of Russia and Poland. Other questions cut in the opposite direction. Rav Breuer wanted membership restricted to Jews who belonged to separate Orthodox communities, excluding those who remained affiliated with communal bodies, reflecting the German Orthodox struggle for formal separation from religiously mixed communal structures. But that didn’t fit the communal realities of every country. Eastern European delegates objected — to them, that wasn’t where the threat lay. According to the research of Rabbi Dovid Kamenetsky, one delegate, Rav Avraham Abelie Schnur of Tarnow, proposed establishing Eastern schools that combined Torah and secular studies. According to one account, a Warsaw philanthropist raised the stakes by offering 50,000 rubles toward a modern school modeled after Rav Hirsch’s Frankfurt system. The hall erupted. Delegates who had arrived to unite Torah Jewry were suddenly fighting over which community’s defensive strategy would define the other. In a private letter, Rav Yitzchak Isaac Halevy called the conference “marvelous,” but acknowledged how hard-won that result had been: Behind the scenes, he had worked ceaselessly to soften Rav Chaim’s demands on one side and Rav Breuer’s on the other. That exposed a problem larger than the argument over secular studies. An organization created to unite very different Orthodox communities could succeed only if joining forces did not mean surrendering the authority of each community to determine its own religious life. The question was not only whether the German model would travel east. It was whether Agudah itself would become a new central authority — in effect, a super-rabbinate — standing above the rabbanim and communities it had been created to serve. The irony would emerge a decade later, when German-born Rabbi Dr. Leo Deutschlander used that same Yekkishe organizational discipline to develop Sarah Schenirer’s Bais Yaakov network into some 250 schools serving 38,000 girls by 1938. The Eighteen Points were Rav Chaim’s answer to that problem. They attempted to draw the boundary between collective power and centralized religious authority: Agudah could organize, advocate for, and strengthen Torah, but it could not become an independent source of Torah policy. Before traveling to Katowice, Rav Chaim believed those protections had been accepted. In a later letter to the Kopuster Rebbe, Rav Shmaryahu Noach Schneersohn, he described what followed. Two years earlier, he wrote, he had told Agudah’s organizers that he would not join them until the regulations were clearly established. They answered that he could rely on their promise that the conditions would be fulfilled, and he traveled to Katowice on that understanding. “When I arrived,” Rav Chaim wrote to the Kopuster Rebbe, “days passed and the regulations were not signed. I asked why they would not sign, and they answered that they would sign them. So they drew the matter out until most of them had departed. I quarreled with them over the deception.” Rav Rosenheim and others eventually signed, he continued, but the structure had still not been established properly. The number 18 is also attested in a contemporary letter. On 22 Sivan 5672, only days after Katowice, Rav Chaim Ozer referred to the great storm that had swept through the camp and to the decree of the Eighteen Points from the Brisk upper chamber — a pointed allusion to Chazal’s Yud-Ches Devarim . Here again, Rav Chaim Ozer’s 1923 account supplies the other side of the documentary
